thread.title: Sonos Stock Tumbles as CFO's Planned Departure Overshadows Record Earnings

title: Sonos Stock Tumbles as CFO's Planned Departure Overshadows Record Earnings
text:
Sonos Stock Tumbles as CFO’s Planned Departure Overshadows Record Earnings By Feb. 6, 2019 5:50 p.m. ET Order Reprints Courtesy of Sonos Text size
Sonos (ticker: SONO) stock tumbled as wide as 16% afterhours Wednesday before settling to a 5% drop. The multiroom smart-speaker company reported record quarterly earnings and revenue, but announced the retirement of its chief financial officer later this year.
The backstory . Sonos went public last summer after receiving a chilly reception from investors on its roadshow before the initial public offering. The company had been seeking a market valuation around $1.8 billion, but had to settle for about $300 million less. Shares were priced at $15 and surged 33% to $19.91 on the first day of trading on Aug. 2. The next day Sonos stock set its intraday high of $23.60. Then investors turned a deaf ear, and the stock began a long decline, and even traded in the single digits in December and part of Janaury. Shares closed Wednesday at $12.37.
Sonos technology allows users to connect multiple speakers throughout their homes to play the same music simultaneously, and to stream tunes from a range of services including Spotify and Pandora. Sonos speakers also support Amazon.com ’s (AMZN) Alexa virtual assistant, with Alphabet ’s (GOOGL) Google Assistant integration on the way.
Smart speakers have become a crowded space, however, and investors have taken note . Amazon has expanded into more devices , and Apple (AAPL) and Google are increasingly devoting their attention to home audio products, as well.
It’s been an eventful week for Sonos stock already, with a JPMorgan analyst suggesting on Monday that Apple could use its massive cash holdings to acquire Sonos, among other targets. That sent Sonos shares over 8% higher on Monday and Tuesday, before the market stopped putting so much weight on speculation and they dropped over 6% Wednesday.
The plot twist . On Wednesday evening, Sonos reported earnings per share of 55 cents for the fiscal first quarter ended Dec. 31–which includes the all-important holiday-shopping season. That’s versus the Wall Street consensus estimate of 43 cents per share and up 53% from the same period the prior year. Sales in the quarter were up 6%, to a record $496 million, compared with the $491 million that analysts had been looking for. Adjusted Ebitda, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, of $87 million, and net income of $62 million were also both all-time highs for the company.
Sonos also announced that it sold 2.4 million devices in the quarter and that the company’s speakers are now in more than 8 million homes. Sonos Beam–a newly released smart TV soundbar–was the largest source of sales growth in the quarter, surging 42% from a year ago. That growth drowned out a 17% drop in wireless-speaker sales due to fading sales of older products such as the PLAY:3 and PLAY:5. Sales of the year-old Sonos One speaker increased 19%.
“Q1 was another good proof-point that we are doing what we said we’ll do–drive sustainable, profitable growth,” Sonos CEO Patrick Spence said in the company’s earnings announcement. “We have what I believe to be the most compelling long-term hardware and software roadmap since I’ve been at Sonos.”
Moving forward . Sonos shares are down 3% in after-hours trading after initially tumbling as much as 16%. Long-time CFO Michael Giannetto announced his retirement from the company in the earnings release. He called his time at Sonos “truly remarkable” and said that he’s “confident in the future of the business and grateful for the many friends and colleagues I’ve met along the way.” Giannetto, 55 years old and a seven-year Sonos veteran, will continue in his role until a successor is appointed later this year.
Sonos reaffirmed its fiscal 2019 full-year guidance, first released in November, of $83 million to $88 million in adjusted Ebidta on revenue of $1.25 billion to $1.28 billion.
While Sonos showed respectable growth in existing and new products in the quarter, thrift-store shelves are well stocked with consumer gadgets from hyped companies that went public before becoming so-called broken IPOs. That is, the stocks trade for much less than their IPO offering price.
Action camera-maker GoPro (GPRO) went public on June 26, 2014, at $24 a share, peaked at $93.85 on Oct. 7 that year, and on Wednesday closed at $5.15. Wearable-smart-devices firm Fitbit (FIT) went public June 18, 2015, at $20, peaked on Aug. 5 at $51.64, and closed Wednesday at $6.43.
Sonos’ rhetorical focus on “sustainable, profitable growth” makes it clear that Spence and the company’s management have these cautionary tales in mind. But investors can’t ignore a CFO jumping ship at a key moment in the young company’s public market story.
